summary: Proposes rules for assigning Top-Level Aggregation and Next-Level Aggregation identifiers in the IPv6 aggregatable address format. It was a proposal for how address space would be handed out. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Think of how a postal system hands out zip codes and street ranges. This proposed rules for handing out parts of new internet addresses in an orderly way.

questions: what are tla and nla in ipv6
how were ipv6 aggregatable addresses assigned
subtitle: Rules for distributing the first layer of IPv6 address space.

tldr.problem: IPv6 introduced a hierarchical address structure with Top-Level Aggregation (TLA) and Next-Level Aggregation (NLA) identifiers. The internet needed clear rules for who could receive these valuable address blocks and how they should be managed.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes assignment rules for TLA and NLA identifiers, restricting TLA assignments to organizations providing transit services (not leaf sites), requiring proof of IPv6 capability, and mandating public registration of all assignments.
tldr.outcome: These proposed rules aimed to keep the routing table manageable by limiting the number of top-level prefixes while allowing hierarchical address allocation to scale. The rules were intended as input to IANA and regional registries for the first two years of IPv6 deployment.

facts.label: Initial scope
facts.value: First two years of IPv6 deployment

today: RFC 2450 is Informational and proposed rules for IPv6 address allocation intended for the first two years of IPv6 deployment. The IPv6 addressing landscape has evolved significantly since 1998, and current practice differs from these proposals. Organizations now apply for IPv6 address space through regional internet registries using updated policies developed over the years of actual IPv6 deployment.

sections.title: IPv6 Address Hierarchy
sections.content:
IPv6 introduces an aggregatable global unicast address format designed to support both provider-based and exchange-based address aggregation. The address format divides a 128-bit address into hierarchical fields: a 13-bit Top-Level Aggregation (TLA) Identifier, an 8-bit Reserved field, a 24-bit Next-Level Aggregation (NLA) Identifier, a 16-bit Site-Level Aggregation (SLA) Identifier, and a 64-bit Interface Identifier.

The 13-bit TLA field allows for 8,192 top-level identifiers. This size was an engineering compromise: smaller would not support enough top-level organizations, while larger would exceed what current routing technology could reasonably handle. The design supports growth: the reserved field can be extended into the TLA or NLA space if routing technology improves.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 addresses are divided into chunks like a postal code system: TLA is like a country, NLA is like a state, SLA is like a city, and the rest is like a street address. We need rules for who gets TLA codes.

sections.title: Limiting Routing Table Size
sections.content:
The primary motivation for these assignment rules is to keep the Internet's default-free routing table within manageable size. IPv4 routing tables at the time contained approximately 50,000 prefixes and were already showing signs of strain. The 13-bit TLA field allows up to 8,192 prefixes in the core routing table, with a reasonable safety margin below IPv4's current size.

Internet topology is complex, with routers seeing the same prefix announced via many different paths. The technical requirement was to choose a TLA size that could support additional topology complexity and a considerably larger internet than IPv4, while staying well below what was already pushing the limits of existing routing technology.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet routers need to remember all the big address chunks. If there are too many, routers slow down and the internet breaks. So we can't hand out too many TLA codes.

sections.title: Assignment Rules for TLA IDs
sections.content:
The RFC proposes that TLA IDs be assigned only to organizations providing transit topology, not to leaf sites even if multi-homed. Transit providers carry traffic between multiple networks and are the only organizations assigned top-level prefixes. The IANA assigns small blocks of TLA IDs to regional registries, which in turn assign them to qualifying organizations. The IANA may also assign TLA IDs directly for experimental activities like the 6bone.

Organizations receiving TLA IDs must demonstrate the ability to provide native IPv6 service within 3 months, have a verifiable track record of providing Internet transit, pay registration fees, provide registry services for the address space they control, report periodically on utilization, and make all assignments publicly available. Organizations failing to meet these requirements may have their TLA assignments revoked.
sections.plainLanguage: You can only get a TLA code if you're a big company that carries traffic for lots of other networks. You have to prove you can actually use it within 3 months and tell everyone publicly what you give out.

sections.title: Two-Stage Allocation Process
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a two-stage allocation process. In the first stage, organizations receive a Sub-TLA ID carved from TLA ID 0x0001. When an organization has assigned more than 90% of its NLA space under the Sub-TLA, it can request and receive a full TLA ID. The Sub-TLA ID need not be returned. This approach allows gradual growth and prevents wasteful hoarding of address space.

Registries may initially assign only a fraction of the NLA ID space for a particular TLA to an organization. When that organization has assigned more than 90% of its allocation, it can request additional NLA space. Registries are encouraged to use "slow start" allocation procedures similar to CIDR practices in IPv4, balancing routing aggregation efficiency with allocation flexibility.
sections.plainLanguage: New companies start small with a Sub-TLA. When they use up most of what they got, they can ask for a full TLA. This stops companies from sitting on address space they don't use.

sections.title: NLA ID Assignment and Hierarchy
sections.content:
Next-Level Aggregation IDs are used by TLA ID holders to create addressing hierarchies and identify sites. Organizations holding TLA IDs are responsible for registry duties for the NLA IDs they assign. Each organization assigned an NLA ID must in turn assume registry duties for the next level, creating a cascading registration requirement.

The RFC leaves the bit layout design of NLA ID space to each TLA holder, allowing customized hierarchies appropriate to each organization's network. Organizations can assign the upper bits of NLA space to create addressing hierarchies (for better routing aggregation) or use flat assignment (for easier allocation and flexibility). This balance between aggregation efficiency and operational flexibility is left to each provider's design.
sections.plainLanguage: Companies with a TLA get to decide how to split their address space among their customers. They might organize by region, by customer size, or any way they want. They have to tell the registry what they handed out.
